_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-15) first version. The bible's Harrowgate Junction is renamed Skelbrook Junction: the name lookup found Harrowgate one letter from Marrowgate, a place in s2e14.
title: When the Oracle Is Down
setting: a sleeper train between two capitals

post.author: u/night_steward_liesl
post.title: I'm the night steward on a sleeper train. At 01:58 our assistant told the man in berth 14 to change at a station that closed in 2019. At 02:48 he was standing at the door with his bag.

blocks.text: I'm Liesl, night steward on the Saraband, the sleeper train between the two capitals: out at 22:40, in at 07:15. I make up the berths, the fold-down beds in each cabin, and I sit up all night in coach C.

Passengers can ask our assistant questions on their phones, in eleven languages. Behind it is a language model, a program that reads text and writes text back. A company called a provider runs the model and sells its use.

The model can't see our timetable. So the app gives it a tool: a small job the model can ask the app to do, like a button it asks us to press. Ours, the timetable tool, looks up tonight's real connections at each stop.

Sometimes the provider refuses instead of answering. Then the app tries again, in steps. It waits about 1 second and asks again. If that fails, it waits about 2 seconds and asks once more. Asking again is called a retry, and making each wait longer is called backoff. Each wait gets a small random extra, so phones that failed together don't ask again at once.

Each try gets up to 30 seconds to answer; that limit is called a timeout. If the third try fails too, the app stops asking our provider and asks a fallback instead: a smaller model at a second company, kept for emergencies. Mr Pashley, who built the app, wired it in from the start.

We launched in February. In eight months his log shows 11 errors, refusals from our provider, each over within 3 seconds. Every time, a retry got through. The fallback never answered a single passenger. Nobody had tested it.
Tonight the errors began at 01:12 and lasted until 03:24.

At 01:58 the man in berth 14 asked how to reach Whinmoor by morning. This is the app's record of his question. Each line shows the time, who was asked, what came back (529 is the provider's number for too busy right now), and what the app did next.

01:58:00.00  main      529 overloaded   wait 1.13 s
01:58:01.33  main      529 overloaded   wait 2.21 s
01:58:03.74  main      529 overloaded   give up
01:58:03.94  fallback  question sent, tools: none
01:58:06.54  fallback  "Change at Skelbrook Junction,
                        platform 2, at 02:50."
The Saraband hasn't stopped at Skelbrook since the station closed in 2019. We still pass through it at 02:50, slowly, on the bend.
At 02:48 I found him at the door of coach B with his bag, watching for a platform that has no lamps.

blocks.label: berth14_0158.png

diagram.aria: Liesl's drawing of the app's record for berth 14's question, 01:58:00 to 01:58:08. The main provider is asked three times, at 01:58:00.00, 01:58:01.33 and 01:58:03.74, and each time a 529 comes back 0.2 seconds later. Between the tries the app waits 1.13 seconds, then 2.21 seconds. At 01:58:03.94 the fallback gets the question with no tool, and at 01:58:06.54 it has answered: change at Skelbrook Junction, platform 2, at 02:50.

blocks.caption: Drawn from the app's record. Three tries to our provider, each refused with a 529 in 0.2 seconds, with waits of 1.13 and 2.21 seconds between them. At 01:58:03.94 the app gave up and sent the question to the fallback, with no tool. Its answer was finished at 01:58:06.54.

blocks.text: I got him to Whinmoor from the printed connections sheet: the real change was Calderwick at 03:41. At 03:30, with the errors over, I asked the app his question again. It said Calderwick, platform 4.

Mr Pashley found why the fallback had no tool. The second company expects tools described in a different form. Between our app and it sits an adapter, a small program that rewrites each question we send into that form. It has no rule for our timetable tool, so it quietly leaves it out. With no tool, the fallback answered from memory: from what it learned in training, which included years of old timetables.
The assistant goes back on tomorrow night. Mr Pashley says the retries did exactly as told. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing aboard is haunted, though a junction that opens again at 01:58 comes close. A 529 is how some providers say they are overloaded: Anthropic's name for it is overloaded_error, and its errors page says it can happen under high traffic across all users. Providers also keep a status page, a public page saying what is broken right now and when it was fixed. Three questions. How fast did each 529 come back tonight? In eight months, how long was the longest error, and did anything ever reach the fallback before tonight? And what exactly did the fallback receive along with his question?

replies.author: u/night_steward_liesl
replies.text: Each 529 came back in 0.2 seconds, on every line. The longest error before tonight lasted 2.6 seconds, on 3 June, and the third try got through, as always. Nothing ever reached the fallback. The adapter keeps its own log. For 01:58 it says: tools offered 1, tools sent 0, timetable skipped, no rule for a field that takes a station name or a station code. Our standing instructions, the text sent with every question, did go across, including the line that says always check connections with the timetable tool.

comments.author: u/five_retries_brenzett
comments.text: Two retries is too few. Your 11 old errors were over in 3 seconds because the retries only ever gave them 3 seconds. Five retries with backoff, waiting 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds, gives the provider over half a minute to come back, and providers usually do. The fallback is a smaller, weaker model on a path nobody uses, so it should be the very last resort, not the third try. Five with backoff would have ridden tonight out on the model you trust.

replies.author: u/night_steward_liesl
replies.text: Mr Pashley likes this. He says it's one number in the settings.

comments.author: u/one_more_spare_ondrej
comments.text: Trains carry a spare crew for a reason. Two companies down at the same moment is rare; three is rarer still. Put a third provider behind the fallback, so there is always one more model in line to answer.

reply.prompt: The assistant goes back on tomorrow night. What should the Saraband change before the next outage? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Test the fallback with the same questions and tools, and have it say when it can't check.
options.part2: Mr Pashley wrote down the questions passengers really ask, with the right answers from the timetable, and sent them to the fallback as it was. It used no tool on any connection question, because it never had one, and answered every one from memory. He taught the adapter to rewrite the field that takes a station name or a station code, and ran them again: the fallback asked the timetable every time. Then he took the tool away on purpose, and it said: I can't check connections right now. Please ask the steward in coach C. We replayed tonight on a test phone. The three tries failed by 01:58:03.94; the fallback asked the timetable and had answered by 01:58:07.14: change at Calderwick, platform 4, at 03:41, for the 04:05 to Whinmoor. The test runs every Monday now, and before every change to the app.
options.senior: A fallback you have never run is a guess. Test it the way you test the main path: the same questions, the same tools, the same marks, on a schedule and before every change, because the second company and your adapter both change under you. Check that every tool arrives, and fail loudly when one is dropped. And give the fallback an honest way down: when it can't use a tool it needs, it says what it can't do and who can, instead of answering from training. Anthropic's errors page says 529 means the API is temporarily overloaded, and that it can happen under high traffic across all users: an outage you don't cause and can't shorten. The retries and the switch were fine; the path they switched to was the part nobody had seen.

options.text: Retry the main provider five times with backoff before ever switching to the fallback model.
options.verdict: Longer waits, the same stale answer
options.part2: Mr Pashley set five retries, waiting 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds, each with its small random extra. We replayed tonight on a test phone. The phone showed its dots for over half a minute. At 01:58:32.81 the fallback got the question, still with no tool, and at 01:58:35.41 it said: change at Skelbrook Junction, platform 2, at 02:50. To outlast the 86 minutes left of tonight's outage from 01:58, the app would have needed 13 retries, the last wait over an hour, and the answer would have come at 04:14, after the train had passed Calderwick.
options.senior: Retries are for short failures; a long outage outlasts any count. With waits that double from 1 second, n retries wait about 2 to the power n, minus 1, seconds: five give 31 seconds, thirteen over two hours. Meanwhile every passenger stares at a spinner, and every phone asking again adds load to a provider that has said it is overloaded (Dead Letter s6e01, Wait Longer). And if a stream breaks partway, a retry can mean paying for the whole answer again. Keep two or three quick retries for the short blips, then switch, and have the app stop asking a provider that keeps failing for a while, the circuit breaker of Dead Letter s6e02, The Breaker Box. More retries only delay the moment the untested path runs.

options.text: Give each try a longer timeout, so a slow provider has time to answer before we give up.
options.part2: Mr Pashley raised each try's timeout from 30 to 90 seconds. We replayed tonight on a test phone, and nothing moved: each 529 came back in 0.2 seconds, so no try ever came near its timeout. The fallback had the question at 01:58:03.94, with no tool, and at 01:58:06.54 it named Skelbrook again. Then we pretended the provider went silent instead, taking the question and saying nothing. Three silent tries now took 273.34 seconds before the fallback was asked, where 30-second tries had taken 93.34.
options.senior: A timeout only matters when nothing comes back. Tonight the provider answered fast, with a refusal, so a longer wait changed nothing. When a provider does go silent, a longer timeout makes each passenger wait longer before the fallback. For a streamed answer, split the timeout in two: a short one for the first word, set a little above how long first words normally take, and a longer one for the whole answer. A provider that has sent nothing in 5 seconds is usually not about to start. Anthropic's page names a separate error, 504 timeout_error, for a request that timed out while being processed, and recommends streaming for long requests.

options.text: Add a third provider after the fallback, so there is always one more model to answer.
options.part2: Mr Pashley signed up a third company and put it behind the fallback, with its own adapter. We replayed tonight on a test phone. The third provider was never asked: the second company was up all night, and its model had answered by 01:58:06.54, with no tool, Skelbrook again. The new path had never answered a passenger either. Nobody had tested it.
options.senior: A third provider protects against two companies failing at once, which does happen, so it isn't wrong. But tonight's failure wasn't a missing model; it was a fallback that answered badly, and a third in line is never reached while the second is answering. Every extra provider is another adapter, another set of tool formats and another path that runs only in emergencies. Test the second before you add a third, and when you add one, put it in the same weekly test.

sim.title: Replay the 01:58 question through the outage
sim.lede: You're Liesl, replaying berth 14's question, which is sent at 01:58:00.00. No real model runs here: every answer comes from two stated timetables. Tonight's says change at Calderwick, platform 4, at 03:41, for the 04:05 to Whinmoor. The one in the fallback's training, from before 2019, says change at Skelbrook Junction, platform 2, at 02:50. The main provider's outage runs from 01:12:00 to 03:24:00, or, for a short failure like the 11 before tonight, for 3 seconds from 01:58:00.00; a try sent inside it fails. A fast failure is a 529 back in 0.2 seconds; a silent one sends nothing until the try's timeout. Waits double from 1 second, each with a small extra the app drew for this question, from its record: 0.13, 0.21, 0.07, 0.18, 0.02, 0.24, 0.11, 0.05, 0.16, 0.09, 0.20, 0.03, 0.14 seconds. A model with the timetable tool gives its first word 1.4 seconds after it is asked and finishes at 3.2; without a tool, 0.8 and 2.6. You open at 01:11, with the main provider up and nothing asked yet.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Ask and watch three 529s, waits of 1.13 and 2.21 seconds, and the fallback's Skelbrook answer at 01:58:06.54. Set the outage to 3 seconds: the third try, at 01:58:03.74, gets through. Back to tonight, give the fallback the timetable tool and read Calderwick at 01:58:07.14; take it away with the honest refusal on and read what it says instead. Try 5 and 13 retries, a 90-second timeout, and a silent outage. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing came back from 2019. Tonight's outage was the first in eight months to outlast two retries, so the fallback answered a passenger for the first time. The adapter had left out the timetable tool it couldn't rewrite, and with no tool the fallback answered from timetables it learned in training.

steps.title: Two retries cleared every short failure.
steps.text: A retry happens in steps. First the app sends the question. Second the provider refuses, here with a 529 in 0.2 seconds. Third the app waits, 1 second plus a small random extra (that extra is called jitter, from Wait Longer), and asks again. Fourth, if that fails, it waits 2 seconds plus an extra and asks a third time. So the third try is never sent before 3.4 seconds (0.2 + 1 + 0.2 + 2), and every error over within 3 seconds was cleared: all 11 in eight months, the longest 2.6 seconds. Tonight the third try went at 01:58:03.74. Retry only errors that may clear by themselves. Anthropic's errors page says to retry a 500 api_error with exponential backoff, and its SDK, its ready-made code library, retries connection errors, rate limits (429) and 5xx server errors, 529 among them, twice by default. A 400 invalid_request_error means your own request is wrong; sending it again sends the same mistake. What can go wrong: retries buy seconds, not hours.

steps.title: Tonight outlasted any sensible count.
steps.text: The outage ran from 01:12 to 03:24, 132 minutes; at 01:58 there were 86 minutes, 5,160 seconds, left. Waits that double from 1 second add up to about 2 to the power n, minus 1, seconds after n retries: 5 retries wait 31 seconds (the fallback gets the question at 01:58:32.81), 12 wait 4,095, and only 13, at 8,191, get past 03:24. Then the main model answers at 04:14:36.63, after the train has left Calderwick. Each passenger watches a spinner the whole time, and every phone asking again adds load to a provider that has said it is overloaded: the retry storm of Dead Letter s6e01, Wait Longer. What can go wrong: a long outage turns more retries into longer silence. Dead Letter s6e02, The Breaker Box, covers the circuit breaker that stops asking a failing provider for a while.

steps.title: The fallback ran for the first time, without its tool.
steps.text: A switch to another company happens in steps. First the app builds its request: the standing instructions, the question, and the timetable tool. Second the adapter rewrites it into the second company's form, the messages first and then each tool. Third, a tool with a field that takes a station name or a station code has no rule, so the adapter skips it without a word: tools offered 1, tools sent 0. Fourth the fallback model reads instructions telling it to check connections with a tool it doesn't have, and writes anyway, from training, where the Saraband still stops at Skelbrook at 02:50. What can go wrong: every step on a path that never runs can break unseen. This was not a model that sounded different; it was the same question answered without the facts.

steps.title: Two timeouts for a streamed answer.
steps.text: Streaming, from a2e07, sends the answer word by word. It can fail in two places: before the first word, or partway through. So a careful app keeps two timeouts: a short one for the first word, set a little above how long first words normally take, and a longer one for the whole answer. Tonight neither mattered, because each 529 came back in 0.2 seconds. They matter when a provider goes silent: three silent tries of 30 seconds each, with tonight's waits, take 93.34 seconds before the fallback is asked; at 90 seconds a try, 273.34; with a 5-second wait for the first word, 18.34. What can go wrong: a first-word timeout set too tight cuts off slow but healthy answers.

steps.title: Status pages, and failing honestly.
steps.text: A provider's status page says what is broken and when it was fixed; read it, and record the times beside your own log, as Liesl did with 01:12 and 03:24. Then decide what each path may do. A fallback with every tool can give the same answers, perhaps a little worse. A fallback without one should say what it can't do and who can: I can't check connections right now. Please ask the steward in coach C. Test that behaviour on purpose, with the same questions as the main path, the eval set idea of a5e05, every week and before every change. Build Night G6 builds the general timeouts, retries and breaker; this case adds what is different for models.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn as two tested paths. The passenger app runs the timetable tool itself. It asks the main provider up to three times; during an outage each try comes back 529. Then it sends the question through the adapter, which now rewrites the timetable tool, to the fallback provider's smaller model, tested every Monday with the same questions and tools. Without the tool, the fallback says it can't check.

explain.caption: Read left to right. The app asks the main provider up to three times; during tonight's outage each try came back 529 in 0.2 seconds. Then it switches: the adapter, now with a rule for every tool, passes the question and the timetable tool to the fallback's smaller model. The app itself runs the tool when either model asks. The fallback path is tested every Monday with the same questions and tools, and without the tool it says it can't check.

fix.title: The fix: test the fallback like the main path, and let it say what it can't do
fix.text: Keep the two quick retries for short blips, and retry only errors that may clear by themselves: overloaded, rate-limited and server errors, not a request the provider says is wrong. Then switch to the fallback. Test that path on purpose, with the same questions, the same tools and the same marks as the main path, every week and before every change to the app or the adapter, because the second company's formats change too. Make the adapter fail loudly when it can't rewrite a tool, instead of leaving it out. Give the fallback an honest way down: without a tool it needs, it says I can't check connections right now. Please ask the steward in coach C. Split each try's timeout in two for streamed answers, one for the first word and one for the whole answer. Log which path answered every question, and alert when the fallback starts answering, so the steward knows before a passenger does.

limits: A tested fallback is still a different, smaller model. It may answer worse even with every tool, and a weekly test only shows last Monday's behaviour. Keep its job narrow, and say in the app when the backup is answering.
An honest I can't check still leaves the passenger with one steward at night. Degrading honestly moves the work to people; plan for how many questions they can take during a long outage.

Switching on every error hides your own mistakes. If a new version of the app sends a request the provider rejects as wrong, the fallback will answer every question and the main path can stay broken for days. Switch only on the provider's errors, and alert whenever the fallback answers.

explain.seniorTake: Assume every model provider will fail, sometimes for seconds and sometimes for hours. Retry a little, and only errors that may clear by themselves: overloaded, rate-limited, server errors. Don't retry a request the provider calls wrong; it usually fails the same way again. Keep the retries short so a blip is hidden and a long outage is not dragged out, and stop asking a provider that keeps failing. Then switch to a fallback, and treat that path as production, not insurance: the same questions, the same tools and the same marks, tested on a schedule and before every change, with the adapter failing loudly when it can't carry a tool. Decide in advance what each path may say, so a path missing a tool says what it can't do instead of answering from training. For streamed answers keep two timeouts, one for the first word and one for the whole answer. Log which path answered, alert when the fallback starts, and read the provider's status page beside your own log.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: 529 overloaded_error
realWorld.text: Anthropic's errors page lists 529 - overloaded_error: The API is temporarily overloaded, and warns: 529 errors can occur when the API experiences high traffic across all users. It is an error from the provider's side that may clear by itself, which is what makes it worth a short retry.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: retry some errors, not others
realWorld.text: For 500 - api_error, the page says: Retry the request with exponential backoff. For 400 - invalid_request_error it says: There was an issue with the format or content of your request. And it says the official SDK automatically retries transient failures (such as connection errors, rate limits, and 5xx server errors) with exponential backoff, twice by default, honoring the retry-after header when present.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: errors in a stream, and long requests
realWorld.text: The same page says that when receiving a streaming response, an error can occur after the API returns a 200 response, so a stream needs its own error handling. It lists 504 - timeout_error for a request that timed out while processing, and advises the streaming Messages API for long-running requests, especially those over 10 minutes.

realWorld.title: OpenAI, 11 December 2024: about four hours down
realWorld.text: OpenAI's status page write-up says that between 3:16 PM PST and 7:38 PM PST on December 11, 2024, all OpenAI services experienced significant degradation or complete unavailability. The cause: a new telemetry service configuration that unexpectedly generated massive Kubernetes API load across large clusters, overwhelming the control plane and breaking DNS-based service discovery. No count of retries outlasts four hours and 22 minutes.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: what it changed
realWorld.text: The write-up says all infrastructure-related configuration changes moving forward will follow a robust phased rollout process, and that OpenAI will implement break-glass mechanisms to ensure that engineers can access Kubernetes API servers in any circumstances. For a team that calls a provider, the lesson is the other side: plan for hours, not seconds.

asked: How do you handle a model provider outage?
How do you know your fallback works?
interview.answer: I split it by length. Short blips I hide with two or three retries, waits that double with a little randomness, and only on errors that may clear by themselves: overloaded (529 on Anthropic's API), rate-limited (429) and server errors (5xx). A request the provider calls wrong, a 400, I don't retry or fall back on; it is usually my bug (or a spend limit I set), so I alert. Long outages I don't try to outwait: after the quick retries I switch to a fallback, a second model, ideally at a second provider, and I stop asking the failing one for a while with a circuit breaker. For streamed answers I keep two timeouts, one for the first token and one for the whole answer. Then the part most teams skip: the fallback is production. I run the same eval set through it, with the same tools, every week and before every change, and I check that every tool actually reaches it, because adapters between providers' formats can drop what they can't translate. I decide what each path may say: one missing a tool says what it can't do instead of answering from training. I log which path answered every request, alert when the fallback starts answering, and keep the provider's status page next to my own graphs.

terms.def: A night train with beds, so passengers sleep on the way. The Saraband runs between two capitals, out at 22:40 and in at 07:15.
The person who looks after passengers on a train: making up beds, answering questions, waking people for their stop. Liesl is the Saraband's night steward.
A fold-down bed in a sleeper train's cabin. The man in berth 14 asked how to reach Whinmoor.
A station where railway lines meet, so passengers can change trains. Skelbrook Junction closed in 2019; the Saraband passes it at 02:50.
A train you can change onto at a stop. Tonight's to Whinmoor: change at Calderwick at 03:41, platform 4, for the 04:05.
A program that reads text and writes text back, one likely word at a time, like a phone's next-word suggestions grown huge (a1e01).
A company that runs language models and sells their use (a1e03). The Saraband's assistant uses a main provider and, as its fallback, a second company.
A small job your app offers a model, like a button it can ask you to press. The model asks; your app runs it and sends back the result (a2e05).
The Saraband app's tool that looks up tonight's real connections at each stop. One of its fields takes a station name or a station code.
A reply saying a request could not be served, with a number and a type, such as 529 overloaded_error, in place of an answer.
Anthropic's status code for overloaded_error: the API is temporarily overloaded, for example under high traffic across all users (a2e01).
Anthropic's error type for an overloaded API. Without streaming it arrives as a 529; during a stream, as an error event (a2e07). Worth a short retry.
The error for going over a rate limit, a cap on requests or tokens in a stretch of time (a2e01). Worth retrying after a wait.
Anthropic's error for something unexpected inside its own systems. Its errors page says to retry it with exponential backoff.
Usually a problem with your request's format or content; Anthropic also uses it for a spend limit you set (a6e01). Sending it again gets the same refusal.
The error for a problem with your API key, such as malformed, revoked or expired. Retrying with the same key won't help.
The error for a request over the size limit. Retrying the same request won't help.
Anthropic's error for a request that timed out while being processed. Its page suggests streaming for long requests.
Shorthand for the status codes from 500 to 599, which mean the server's side failed, not your request.
Asking again after a try fails. Worth it for errors that may clear by themselves; useless for a request that is wrong (a2e01, s6e01).
Making each wait before a retry longer than the last. The Saraband's app waits about 1 second, then about 2 (s6e01, Wait Longer).
Backoff where each wait doubles: 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds. After n retries the waits add up to about 2 to the power n, minus 1, seconds.
A small random extra on each wait, so callers that failed together don't all ask again at the same instant (s6e01). Tonight's: 0.13 and 0.21 seconds.
How long a caller waits for an answer before giving up on a try. The Saraband's app gave each try 30 seconds.
A second model, ideally at a second provider, that your code switches to when the first fails (a2e08). It only helps if it has been tested.
A small program that rewrites a request into another provider's form. The Saraband's had no rule for the timetable tool, so it left it out.
How a model learned, from a huge amount of text, before anyone used it (a1e01). What it learned can be years out of date, like an old timetable.
The text sent with every question telling the model what it is for, the system prompt of a2e01. The Saraband's says to check connections with the timetable tool.
A time when a service can't serve requests. Tonight the main provider's ran from 01:12 to 03:24, 132 minutes.
A provider's public page saying what is broken right now and when it was fixed, so customers can match it with their own logs.
Receiving a model's answer in small pieces as it is written, instead of all at once at the end (a2e07).
How long to wait for the first piece of a streamed answer before giving up on a try, set a little above how long first words normally take.
How long to wait for the whole of an answer, from sending the request to its last word.
How long from sending a request until the first piece of the answer arrives, also called TTFT (a2e07).
A failure where the provider takes the request and sends nothing back, so each try lasts until its timeout.
Software development kit: a provider's ready-made code library for calling its API. Anthropic's retries some errors twice by default.
So many callers retrying that the retries themselves keep a struggling server down (s6e01).
Code that stops calling a service that keeps failing for a while, then tries it again carefully. Dead Letter s6e02, The Breaker Box, covers it.
Questions with known good answers and a rule for marking each reply, run on purpose to test a model or a path (a5e05).
When part of a system fails, saying plainly what it can't do now and who can help, instead of giving an answer it can't check.
Measurements a system collects about itself and sends somewhere to be watched, such as how busy each part is.
Software that runs and manages many programs across many servers. OpenAI's 2024 outage began in its Kubernetes clusters.
The part of a system like Kubernetes that decides where programs run and keeps track of them, as opposed to the programs doing the work.
Domain Name System: the internet's phone book, turning names into the numbers computers use to find each other. Inside a cluster, programs use it to find each other too.
Putting a change in front of a small part of a system first, then more, so a bad change hurts little before it is caught.
An emergency way in, kept for when normal access fails, like a key behind glass.
Pacific Standard Time, the clock on the west coast of North America in winter, eight hours behind UTC.
The course's hands-on build of timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, a circuit breaker and a token bucket.
The international standard for information security management. Annex A lists controls such as A.8.14, redundancy of information processing facilities, and A.8.6, capacity management.
An audit report on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. A1.2 covers the protections and recovery infrastructure behind availability.

atWork: Look for a fallback that was wired in once and has never run. It is a common pattern: a second model, often at a second provider, added to a config file when the feature launched, then left alone, because the main provider's short failures always clear on a retry. Ask four things. When did the fallback last answer a real request, and what did it say? Does it receive the same tools and instructions as the main path, or does something between your app and the second provider quietly leave parts out? Which errors make your code retry, and which make it switch: does a request the provider calls wrong ever reach the fallback? And what does each path say when it can't check something it needs to? If the answers are thin, run your eval set through the fallback with the same tools this week, and add it to the schedule. Build Night G6 builds the general timeouts, retries and circuit breaker underneath. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, Annex A control A.8.14 (redundancy of information processing facilities) expects redundancy sufficient to meet availability requirements, and an untested backup path is hard to show as sufficient; A.8.6 (capacity management) covers the capacity you depend on, including a provider's. If you report under SOC 2, availability criterion A1.2 covers the recovery infrastructure you design, operate and monitor, which a scheduled fallback test supports. Building the test in from the first release is far cheaper than proving the backup works for the first time during an audit or an outage.

recall.prompt: Your bank's support assistant calls one model provider. On errors it asks twice more, then switches to a backup model at another company, added a year ago and never used. Questions about balances need a lookup function that the main model calls. What would you do before the next long outage, and why?

keyIdeas.idea: Run the backup path on purpose before it is needed, with the same questions as the main path
Check that the function and instructions actually reach the backup model; an adapter may drop what it can't translate
Without the lookup, the backup should say it can't check instead of answering from memory

recall.model: Test the fallback before you need it: run the same questions as the main path, your eval set, through the backup model on purpose, with the right answers to mark it against, and do it every week and before every change. Check that the balance lookup and the standing instructions actually arrive: the adapter that rewrites requests into the other company's form may have dropped tools it can't translate, and nothing will tell you until it runs. Then decide what the backup does without the lookup: it should say so, that it can't check balances right now and who can, rather than answer from memory. A year of quick retries succeeding proves nothing about a path that has never run.

recall.prompt: Which of these errors from Anthropic's API is worth a short retry with backoff?
options: 400 invalid_request_error: an issue with the format or content of the request
529 overloaded_error: the API is temporarily overloaded
401 authentication_error: the API key is malformed, revoked or expired
413 request_too_large: the request is over the size limit
recall.why: A 529 comes from the provider's side and may clear by itself, so a short retry with backoff can succeed; Anthropic's SDK retries such transient failures twice by default. The other three are about your own request or key: sending the same thing again gets the same refusal.

recall.prompt: Your assistant streams its answers. Normally they start within 2 seconds and finish within 20. Your app has one timer: 120 seconds for the whole call, three tries, then a fallback. Tonight the provider accepts every request and sends nothing back. What do users see, and how would you set the timers?

keyIdeas.idea: Keep two timeouts: one for the first piece of the answer and one for the whole answer
With one long timer, every user waits the full timer on each try, about six minutes, before the fallback
Set each from what is normal: a little above usual first-word and total times

recall.model: With one 120-second timer, each try waits the full two minutes for an answer that never comes, so three tries mean about six minutes of nothing before the fallback is even asked. Use two timeouts instead: a time to first token limit of about 5 seconds, a little above the usual 2, and a total limit a little above the slowest normal answer, say 30 seconds. A provider that has sent nothing in 5 seconds is usually not about to start, so three silent tries cost about 15 seconds plus the waits, and a slow but healthy answer still finishes. Set both from measured times, not guesses.

recall.prompt: Waits double from 1 second (1, 2, 4, 8 ...). Leaving out the small random extras and the 0.2 seconds each error takes, how many retries before the waits outlast the 86 minutes (5,160 seconds) left of the outage at 01:58?
recall.why: After n retries the waits add up to 2 to the power n, minus 1, seconds. Twelve give 4,095 seconds, short of 5,160; thirteen give 8,191. The answer would come at about 04:14, more than two hours after the question and after the train has passed Calderwick.

recall.prompt: Mr Pashley raises each try's timeout from 30 to 90 seconds and replays tonight's 01:58 question. When does the fallback get it?
recall.why: Each 529 came back in 0.2 seconds, so no try ever came near a 30-second timeout, let alone 90. The three tries and two waits end at 01:58:03.94 either way. The other times are what a silent outage would cost with 30-second and 90-second tries.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The fallback is tested every Monday with our questions and the timetable tool, and when it can't check, it says so. On 12 January at 23:10 a new version of the app went out. From then, every request to our main provider came back 400 invalid_request_error: the new version sent a field the provider doesn't accept. The app asked twice more each time, then switched, and the fallback answered, correctly, with the tool. Nobody noticed anything until 15 January, when the second company's bill arrived: 1,140 answers in three nights.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What went wrong, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: A 400 means our own request is wrong: retrying it is pointless, so don't retry it
Switch to the fallback only for the provider's own failures, such as overloaded, rate-limited and server errors
The fallback hid the failure: alert when the fallback answers, and watch its share

coldCase.model: The main path was broken by our own release, not by the provider. A 400 invalid_request_error usually says our own request is wrong (the other common cause, a spend limit you set, wasn't it here), so don't retry it: the same request gets the same refusal, and two more tries only add delay. And don't switch on it either: fall back only on the provider's side failures, overloaded, rate-limited and 5xx server errors. Here the fallback worked so well that it hid the bug for three nights, and the bill was the first sign. Log which path answered every question, raise an alert the first time the fallback answers and whenever its share of answers rises, and treat a 400 after a release as a reason to roll that release back.
